profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a mid-sized economic research consulting firm preparing a client-facing executive briefing and technical appendix on a new white paper about nonlinear Phillips curves and chaotic dynamics in optimal monetary policy. The firm has split work between a macro research workstream and a publishing/client-delivery workstream. The meeting is to align on interfaces: what materials the research lead will hand off, what the strategy lead will package for the client, which version of the model outputs will be treated as current, and what counts as a 'final' brief for circulation to the bank client on Thursday. The agenda is to review current status, confirm the handoff for charts and summary language, align on the technical appendix and executive brief dependencies, and confirm who updates the shared deck folder. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on Wednesday deliverables, file handoffs, and ownership of the shared client package.

members.name: Daniel Wu
members.expertise: DSGE modeling, monetary policy analysis, quantitative simulation outputs
members.background: Daniel leads the firm's macro modeling team and previously worked as a research economist at a central bank, where internal memos often circulated with technical backup before polished client packaging.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid re-running simulations unless absolutely necessary, preserve the nuance of the nonlinear model, and keep the team from oversimplifying the findings into a conventional policy-stability story.
hidden_assumptions: When a deliverable is called the 'brief,' it includes the technical appendix and chart notes because clients usually receive the analytical package as one bundle after internal sign-off.
The 'latest model run' refers to the calibrated deterministic simulations produced after last Friday's parameter cleanup, even if an older chart set is still sitting in the shared deck folder.
A chart is 'ready' once the economics are stable and captions identify the parameter cases; visual polish and client formatting can happen downstream without changing substance.
If someone says a file is 'final,' that means analytically final unless a substantive issue is raised, not necessarily publication-formatted or approved for external circulation.

members.name: Priya Shah
members.expertise: Executive briefing production, stakeholder communication, cross-functional delivery coordination
members.background: Priya manages client-facing economics deliverables for financial institutions and came from a strategy consultancy where client teams treated slide-ready materials and version control conventions as the default source of truth.
members.private_state: She wants a smooth client-ready package with no late surprises, minimal technical ambiguity in the briefing, and clear ownership so the Thursday circulation does not slip.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the 'brief,' they mean the 12-slide executive deck for client circulation; appendices are supporting materials delivered only if separately requested or linked later.
The 'latest model run' is whatever outputs have already been reflected in the current shared deck folder labeled v7, because the shared folder is the operational record for delivery.
A chart is only 'ready' when it has final titles, source lines, footnotes, and client-safe wording; analytical stability alone does not make it handoff-complete.
If a package is described as 'final,' that means approved for external circulation and frozen except for typo-level edits.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss getting 'the brief' ready for Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the integrated analytical package: executive summary, technical appendix, chart notes, and model caveats bundled together for internal sign-off before client delivery.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the client-facing executive slide deck only, with any appendix treated as separate optional backup material.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In consulting settings, both people routinely use 'brief' as shorthand for the main deliverable, and because both are talking about Thursday circulation, the overlap sounds complete even though the boundary of what is included differs.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to using 'the latest run' and 'the current charts.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the simulation set generated after Friday's parameter cleanup, including revised convexity cases and updated equilibrium-path figures saved in his team workspace but not yet dropped into the shared delivery folder.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the chart set already embedded in the shared v7 deck from Tuesday morning, which she assumes reflects the latest approved research output.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume there is one obvious most-recent version, and because neither expects a coordination meeting to revisit underlying model files, the phrase 'latest run' feels precise enough on its face.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a chart being 'ready'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Daniel will send 'ready charts' by end of day.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready' means the figures and parameter cases are analytically locked, with provisional labels acceptable because Priya's team will apply house style later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready' means slide-ready for client packaging, including polished titles, legend wording, source note, and a one-line takeaway that can be pasted directly into the deck.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both commonly classify work by readiness status, and each assumes their own criterion is the standard operating meaning; since they are not debating whether the charts exist, the subtle difference in completion standard remains hidden.

misalignment_points.topic: How the shared folder will be updated
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Daniel will 'drop the files in the folder' and Priya will 'pull from there.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to upload a new subfolder with PDFs, a technical note, and raw image exports in his research team's naming convention, expecting Priya to choose what she needs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects Daniel to replace the linked chart files inside the existing client deck asset folder so the deck auto-updates and her associate can lift the exact latest visuals without searching.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both view the shared folder as the common handoff mechanism, so the method difference feels too operationally mundane to spell out; each assumes the other uses the same folder discipline by default.
